hi.decryption: Vatsaraja defeats Dharmapala -> Dhruva defeats Vatsaraja -> Dharmapala holds Kannauj darbar -> Nagabhata II captures Kannauj permanently

fact.en: Trap: Believing the Rashtrakutas won the Tripartite Conflict. They never permanently held Kannauj. Despite multiple military victories over both the Pratiharas and Palas, the Rashtrakutas always returned to the Deccan. The ultimate victors who permanently held Kannauj were the Gurjara-Pratiharas.
fact.hi: Trap: Believing the Rashtrakutas won the Tripartite Conflict. They never permanently held Kannauj. Despite multiple military victories over both the Pratiharas and Palas, the Rashtrakutas always returned to the Deccan. The ultimate victors who permanently held Kannauj were the Gurjara-Pratiharas.

fact.en: Trap: Confusing the sequence of rulers. Vatsaraja was the Pratihara who first defeated Dharmapala, but it was Rashtrakuta king Dhruva who then defeated Vatsaraja. Dharmapala then revived to establish his darbar at Kannauj. Nagabhata II (Pratihara) finally captured Kannauj permanently.
fact.hi: Trap: Confusing the sequence of rulers. Vatsaraja was the Pratihara who first defeated Dharmapala, but it was Rashtrakuta king Dhruva who then defeated Vatsaraja. Dharmapala then revived to establish his darbar at Kannauj. Nagabhata II (Pratihara) finally captured Kannauj permanently.

fact.en: Trap: Assuming Dharmapala permanently ruled Kannauj. Though Dharmapala held a grand darbar at Kannauj and installed Chakrayudha, this was temporary hegemony, not direct administration. Nagabhata II (son of Vatsaraja) subsequently defeated Chakrayudha and captured Kannauj.
fact.hi: Trap: Assuming Dharmapala permanently ruled Kannauj. Though Dharmapala held a grand darbar at Kannauj and installed Chakrayudha, this was temporary hegemony, not direct administration. Nagabhata II (son of Vatsaraja) subsequently defeated Chakrayudha and captured Kannauj.

fact.en: Trap: Confusing the Arab traveler's descriptions. The Arab merchant Sulaiman (c. 851 CE) refers to the Pratiharas as 'Jurz' (Gurjara), the Palas as 'Ruhmi' or 'Dharma', and the Rashtrakutas as 'Balhara'. Do not mix up these references.

fact.en: Trap: Thinking the conflict involved only two powers at any given time. While individual battles were between two powers, the conflict was a continuous three-way struggle — whenever one power weakened the other two, the third power stepped in, preventing any single lasting victory.
